title: Nathan Twining reference in Disclosure Day, with the Twining memo and Majestic 12

tellings.quote: who's head of air material command 1947. He wrote the Twining memo. He was rumored Majestic 12 and 12 people are missing.

plain: Discussing the film Disclosure Day, Jesse Michels points to General Nathan Twining, head of the Air Force's Air Materiel Command in 1947, who wrote the Twining memo, a letter dated September 23, 1947 titled "AMC Opinion Concerning 'Flying Discs'", and who was, Michels says, rumored to belong to Majestic 12, said to be a secret group of twelve officials handling UFO matters. That rumor rests on the MJ-12 papers, a briefing paper that reached a researcher anonymously on film in 1984, which lists "Gen. Nathan F. Twining" among the twelve and says "a covert analytical effort organized by Gen. Twining and Dr. Bush acting on the direct orders of the President" studied a recovered disc, and on a 1954 memo to Twining, reported found at the National Archives in 1985, that says "the President has decided that the MJ-12 SSP briefing should take place" at a White House meeting. Both would place Twining inside such a group only as far as they are genuine: the National Archives says the second memo "poses problems" and FBI copies of both are marked "BOGUS", while some researchers judged them "almost certainly genuine"; the 1947 Twining memo itself is a separate letter on flying discs.

discussion.text: A typed briefing paper dated 18 November 1952, with a Truman memorandum to Secretary Forrestal of 24 September 1947 as its Attachment A, that came to light on a roll of 35mm film Jaime Shandera received anonymously at his Burbank home in 1984 and that he, William Moore and Stanton Friedman then studied; it was made public in 1987. The National Archives and the Truman and Eisenhower Libraries report their searches for it negative. The FBI's Majestic 12 file holds copies sent to it in 1988 and 1991, each marked "BOGUS" by hand, and records that the Air Force Office of Special Investigations "advised on November 30, 1988, that the document was fabricated" and that "the document is completely bogus". Philip Klass called the Truman memo an obvious fraud; Friedman judged the briefing paper and the memo "almost certainly genuine". The briefing paper lists "Gen. Nathan F. Twining" among the twelve members and says "A covert analytical effort organized by Gen. Twining and Dr. Bush acting on the direct orders of the President" judged the recovered disc a short range reconnaissance craft in September 1947. This is the paper behind Michels' "rumored Majestic 12", and Twining's place in the group holds only as far as it is genuine; the Twining memo he also names is the 1947 Air Materiel Command letter on flying discs, a separate document.

A one-page memorandum dated 14 July 1954 from Robert Cutler to General Nathan Twining that Jaime Shandera and William Moore reported finding in July 1985 in Record Group 341, Entry 267, at the National Archives. The Archives says it "poses problems": the series is filed by Top Secret register number and it bears none; its marking "Top Secret Restricted Information" came into use at the National Security Council only under Nixon; it has no letterhead or watermark; the NSC minutes hold no meeting on 16 July 1954; and Cutler was abroad on 14 July 1954. Stanton Friedman judged it "almost certainly genuine", answering that Cutler had left instructions with NSC executive secretary James Lay. The FBI's Majestic 12 file holds a copy marked "BOGUS" by hand. The memo, addressed to General Twining and dated 14 July 1954, says "The President has decid[[ed]] that the [[MJ-12]] SSP br[[ief]]ing should take place during the already sched[[ul]]ed White [[Ho]]use meeting of July 16" (double brackets mark letters illegible in the FBI's copy). It would place Twining inside an MJ-12 briefing, as the rumor Michels mentions has it; it does so only as far as the memo is genuine.
